Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to Swiggy Limited Q2 FY27 Earnings 
Conference Call. All participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and there will be an 
opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should you need assistance 
during the conference, please signal an operator by pressing star and then zero on your touchtone 
phone. Please note that this conference is being recorded. 
 
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Sumant Sharma from the Investor Relations team. Thank 
you, and over to you, sir. 
Sumant Sharma: 
Thank you, Operator. Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Q2 FY27 earnings conference call 
for Swiggy. Our financial results and shareholders’ letter have been published on the exchanges 
and the information pack has been placed in the Investor Relations section of our website, 
www.swiggy.com. 
 
We would like to inform you that the management may make certain comments on the call that 
one could deem forward-looking statements. Specifically, the financial guidance and pro forma 
information that we will provide on this call are management estimates based on certain 
assumptions and have not been subjected to any audit review or examination procedures. Swiggy 
does not guarantee these statements and is not obliged to update them at any time. 
 
Joining us on the call today are Sriharsha Majety – MD and Group CEO; Rahul Bothra – CFO , 
Rohit Kapoor – CEO of Food Marketplace and Nandita Sinha – CEO of Instamart 
 With this brief preamble, let us start the Q&A. Operator, you can please go ahead. 
Moderator: 
Thank you very much. We will now begin with the question-and-answer session. Your first 
question comes from the line of Gaurav Malhotra with Axis Capital. 
Gaurav Malhotra: 
Just a couple of questions on food and quick commerce. So firstly, on food, if you can give us 
some sense on what you're seeing in terms of emerging competition from Rapido, we see Flipkart 
Minutes also doing something in food. So how are you sort of seeing the landscape? 
Sriharsha Majety: 
Hi Gaurav, Harsha here. I'll take that first question. Actually, as of now, only Rapido is live to 
the general public and Flipkart has opened to the public at scale even in Bangalore yet. We are, 
of course, closely watching the market. We happen to be participating in this in the value market 
through our pilots with Toing. 
 
And we've talked about it extensively in our shareholders’ letter as well. I think over the last 4-
5 quarters, we are closely monitoring the business health, the product market fit. And we're quite 
excited by what we are seeing as of now. Competition has begun, but we're able to respond pretty 
strongly both from the Swiggy asset platform as well as the Toing asset. 
 
Our sense, however, as of now, and that's the reason why we're investing in Toing also right now 
is that we do believe that the market can expand if the right proposition offering value to 
consumers while being sustainable can be cracked. For us, it's a specific interest also because 
Toing in some sense for us insurance of a large profit pool at its worst and in addition to a large 
profit pool at its best. 

 
 
 
 
Page 3 of 15 
 
 
And that is the reason why we continue to play for it. We continue to monitor all the health 
metrics and are continuously revising our plans and iterating on the business based on everything 
we know. 
Gaurav Malhotra: 
Got it. In the shareholders’ letter, even in food, you have sort of mentioned about investments 
towards the affordability trust. So, Toing, is where the affordability focus is. So, is there some 
sort of an overlap happening between the food and Toing from an affordability focus 
perspective? 
Sriharsha Majety: 
There is some overlap, but we've also talked about the extent of the overlap and how it's been 
changing with time. Every passing month as we get scale, we're seeing the overlap actually 
improve as in reduce, which is what gives us confidence that it is the opening of a new market. 
 
There is going to be some, but we monitor it closely, and it is a very healthy right now as we 
see. And as it scales, it's starting to get better. The overlap percentage is reducing, which for us 
increases our confidence that this is the opening of a new market. 
Gaurav Malhotra: 
Got it. And just one question on quick commerce. Some of the underlying metrics in quick 
commerce were decent, right in terms of the MTU additions, your throughput per store, those 
sort of moved up. But the delta change in losses seems a little bit on the higher side. So, if you 
could just help us understand that. I understand in the shareholders’ letter, you've given us some 
sense on where the extra margin compression has come from. 
 
But if you can give us some sense on, how should we think about these losses going forward? 
Also, now that you started to sort of refocus on growth, would that also mean that you will be 
getting back into focusing on the Tier-2 markets? 
Nandita Sinha: 
Nandita here. This quarter, we've got back on the growth trajectory. We've had a good quarter 
with a 13.4% QoQ NOV growth. What makes us excited about this growth is the fact that the 
quality of growth has been very good. We've seen our retention metrics go up and our frequency 
metrics have go up by 4% QoQ. We've added 1.3 million MTUs, as you said. 
 
We've built this on the back of habit building, which has been on the back of cohortized user 
bases on which we have done habit building, and we have invested behind our differentiated 
assortment proposition. This makes us confident on the quality of growth that we've been adding. 
 
As a result of this, we believe that as we continue to build the quality of growth, both on the user 
side, which is on building our frequency, habits building our differentiated assortment, which 
has actually given us great results in terms of the retention that we see on the platform and also 
increase the productivity that we have on the throughput of each pod. 
 
This will actually take us towards sustainability and profitable growth. So, this is our journey 
that we will continue to make. We are confident of the quality of growth that we've added in this 
quarter. 
Gaurav Malhotra: 
Got it. And the second question in terms of the Tier 2 markets and how are you thinking about 
it now? 

 
 
 
 
Page 4 of 15 
 
Nandita Sinha: 
We believe that we have laid out our network in terms of T1 and T2 markets. We will continue 
to focus on markets where we are seeing growth in the same manner of building back our 
habituated users and reaching out to them through both the habit building categories like fresh 
and staples as well as extending our differentiated assortment category. 
 
This is how we will build business and the focus will be to continue to build user quality across 
the market as we go forward. 
Moderator: 
The next question comes from the line of Vijit Jain with Citi. 
Vijit Jain: 
In the letter, you mentioned that Toing's success can basically get the food overall marketplace 
growth to 25-30% from the current range of 18-20%. At the moment, would you be closer to the 
lower end of that number, 25% odd? In general, that 7-10% extra growth in GMV terms 
translates to maybe 10-15% higher volumes. Am I roughly in the right ballpark when I look at 
those numbers in that lens? 
Sriharsha Majety: 
I can't answer the specifics of the second part, but to the first part of your question, we would be 
closer to that lower end of that range that we talk. We mentioned in the shareholders’ letter as 
well, we're also learning and getting even more proof points about the business at this time. And 
that's where we are going to have investments range bound while we get even more discovery 
of some key questions that we have. 
Vijit Jain: 
Got it. Harsha, just a related question to that. Now is therefore Toing now at a point where 
shutting this down, calling it an experiment is now not likely at all? Would you be comfortable 
to make that assessment of Toing at this point of time? And if you can talk also about the 
retention cohorts that you're seeing on Toing. 
 
You've mentioned retention cohorts on Instamart at 60% month 1 and so on. So, any colour you 
can give on how the retention cohorts of Toing are doing right now based on whatever the right 
benchmarks for it should be? That will be super helpful. That was my second question. 
Rahul Bothra: 
Hi Vijit, Rahul here. As your question it's an experiment or how it's ready to be scaled, I think 
we have asked for maybe another quarter or two. With enough green shoots we are seeing to be 
able to also call out that this investment is showing the frequency growth that we are hoping for, 
the category extension in terms of new user acquisition to the platform. And more importantly, 
some of the earlier cities turning unit economic positive for the repeat users. 
 
Now you can imagine that in an affordable offering where the average of basket sizes are a 
fraction of, say, the main platform it is extremely hard to build the business because it requires 
significant density. It requires the cost to serve to match the revenue, which is also a fraction of 
the main platform. So our ability to navigate many of this also comes from the fact that we are 
building in the back of the original chassis that is fully expressed in the main platform. 
 
So the incremental overhead that we incur is just on user acquisition. The fixed cost is very, very 
low in this business. It's all discretionary. Therefore, our ability to scale up or dial down is very 
agile in the segment. So you should probably give us another quarter or two before we call out 

 
 
 
 
Page 5 of 15 
 
whether this experiment has worked. But enough we see to be able to give you that direction is 
the right direction. 
Rohit Kapoor: 
Rohit here, just to add to what Rahul said, another notable point is that what you see is mentioned 
in the letter is that a sizable number of restaurants are seeing Toing volumes contribute 
meaningfully to their platform, their restaurant share. So it is not just on the consumer side, but 
also in the cities we are present. If you go and talk to restaurants today, they will talk about the 
two existing players and Toing quite regularly. It's becoming meaningful for restaurants as well. 
Rahul Bothra: 
Just to answer your second question on the retention metrics. One thing we can call out is that 
we are seeing better retention metrics than the core app. Not only the retention metrics are better, 
but the frequency of even the dual appers is 25% higher than the singular app. As I said, the 
metrics look in the right direction. At the same time, we need to continue to scale the business 
with the right business market economics is where the current focus is.  
Sriharsha Majety: 
Building on top of the Swiggy platform and the Swiggy pipes is one of the things that we are 
generally very excited about. That's what he said by saying that it is discretionary and optional 
and even to this quarter or in general, most of our spending is in new user acquisition and 
activation as opposed to any other loaded cost that traditional new business would have to take. 
 
This and the ability to constantly be able to open up the market at a fraction of the cost that new 
insurgence might have is something that motivates us to continue to play and find even better 
answers over the next two quarters. 
Moderator: 
Your next question comes from the line of Sachin Salgaonkar with Bank of America. 
Sachin Salgaonkar: 
I have three questions. First question, what steps, Harsha, Rohit, you guys are taking to avoid 
Toing cannibalizing Swiggy? And I'm asking that because when we look at the growth rates of 
Swiggy and compare that with Zomato, one gets a sense that for the last couple of quarters, they 
are a bit slower. Any specific thing to watch out for, but I would love to understand how you're 
looking at it from that point of view. 
Rohit Kapoor: 
Rohit here. Let me take the question in two parts. On the growth rate, if you see what we’ve 
called out in the letter, that in Sep-26 we were back on 20% plus growth just talking about 
Swiggy. And we see us maintaining the 18-20% stand-alone guidance on Swiggy. On Toing, 2 
out of 3 users that we're seeing are new to platform. 
 
As Rahul mentioned, even on the users who are using both, we are seeing 25% higher orders per 
user. It is doing two or three jobs for us clearly the combined strategy. One is open up the market 
to a new set of consumers who either have very low frequency on food delivery or they're not 
on food delivery. 
 
Point number two is give more choices to consumers on what occasions, which app they want 
to use, and they are showing that they are rewarding that strategy with a higher orders per user 
frequency. And third, obviously, there's a competitive shift in landscape. 

 
 
 
 
Page 6 of 15 
 
 
As Harsha said, that clearly, we see there a robust strategy to participate in the market where 
there is 10 years of legacy of building a food delivery business and new entrants entering. So it's 
insurance we feel, but on the upside, it has significant potential to unlock value in the future. 
Sachin Salgaonkar: 
Clear on that, Rohit. Second question on quick commerce. I see in shareholders' letter, you guys 
have mentioned contribution margin to remain in the range of 0 to -100 bps with sequential 
improvement there on. Is this subject to better retention and maturity of cohorts? I'm asking this 
question because competition is still intense. What points we should look to see that you guys 
will go down and start improving the contribution margin versus contribution margin remaining 
at these levels only? 
Rahul Bothra: 
Yes. What we had called out even in the previous quarter was that we need a bit of reset in terms 
of our growth. And the 0 to -100 basis points guidance that we have given was keeping that 
flexibility in mind. As you have seen, we have grown at a healthy pace of 13% plus in the 
previous quarter and our guidance for the current quarter is also to be able to deliver double-
digit growth on a sequential basis. We will obviously operate within those tight guardrails. 
 
It is important that the users that we have churned out which were unprofitable and the quality 
that we have hence acquired and continue to show better behaviours both from a retention 
frequency delta is something that we want to maintain. And that will ultimately give us a positive 
contribution margin from the existing users that we will operate with. 
 
While the competition intensity remains high, I think as a platform, we have made various steps 
towards getting better customer experience in the market. Therefore, we are very confident of 
being able to do that without worrying about the competition in the market. 
Sachin Salgaonkar: 
Got it. So what you're saying is we should expect an improvement in the revenue as well as 
contribution losses or contribution margin improving going ahead? 
Rahul Bothra: 
So, as I said, it's hard to give a specific number, but what we have guided is for 100 basis points 
improvement in Adjusted EBITDA in the current quarter. 
Sachin Salgaonkar: 
Okay. And that 100 basis points of Adjusted EBITDA has no benefit coming from the move to 
inventory model, right, because the move to inventory model happens mid of next quarter. 
Rahul Bothra: 
That's correct. So we will start the process in the middle of current quarter, and it is expected to 
fully transition over the next two to three quarters. 
Sachin Salgaonkar: 
My last question is and sorry to harp on this, I asked you guys this question in the past also. How 
should we think about the dark store additions and the growth? Because clearly, one of your 
peers had guided to reach 5,000 dark stores. You do see their growth also accelerating and 
outperforming the growth of others in the industry out there. You guys have a decent amount of 
cash on balance sheet. So what would make you guys to change the strategy in terms of adding 
more dark stores and hence, in a way, benefiting from a slightly better growth out there? 
Rahul Bothra: 
I think Sachin, at the cost of repeating, I think we do maintain the fact that store addition is going 
to be a factor of growth, right, because we are present in the 130 plus cities that we are. We don't 

 
 
 
 
Page 7 of 15 
 
have a near-term expectation to increase the geographical coverage. So therefore, the store 
addition, which competition may be doing store city addition is therefore not to be considered 
in our case. 
 
Wherever there is going to be growth and which is maxing out of capacity, we are adding stores. 
So, you will continue to see us expanding the number of stores even in the current quarter as the 
growth continues in those hyper local zip codes. As you can also see from the overall capacity 
utilization, last quarter, we increased it by close to 10% on an orders per day per store. But it 
still leaves sufficient room to continue the growth journey without having to necessarily increase 
the pace of store expansion. From a coverage standpoint in these cities, we are well covered. 
 
So even if you look at the speed metrics, we are best-in-class compared to some of the 
competition out there. From the assortment standpoint as a combination of our larger stores, 
which are the mega stores as well as the hyperlocal normal stores, we are able to provide the 
assortment that is required to get the growth that we are on. So we don't see the need to 
necessarily add a lot many more stores. And as growth continues, you will see that store 
expansion continuing. 
Moderator: 
Your next question comes from the line of Abhisek Banerjee with ICICI Securities. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Just on the store expansion, you just spoke about how you are adding stores wherever you are 
maxing out in terms of capacity. Now could you give us some colour on what that maxing out 
of capacity looks like in terms of orders per dark store per day? So what number do you hit and 
then you have to put up a new store? And what proportion of your total stores would be at that 
kind of a level, if you can give some colour on that. 
Rahul Bothra: 
We typically start the decision to open a new store in that zip code when the store crosses around 
2,000 orders a day. And by the time the store is up, which typically takes 2-3 months, those 
stores start doing roughly 2,300-2,500 orders per day. Every quarter, the pace of expansion, as 
you see if you are adding 5-7% stores, that's the number that are maxing out on capacity, if the 
pace of growth continues at this level. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Understood. The proportion of stores where you have that 2,500-odd throughput of your overall 
store universe. 
Rahul Bothra: 
As I mentioned, every quarter, roughly 5-7% of network is close to that. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Okay. So this is not a cumulative number, right? 
Rahul Bothra: 
No, it changes every quarter. So if you are delivering the growth, say, sequentially on the double-
digit side, you will see more stores getting out of capacity and therefore, the store addition 
becomes a natural outcome. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Understood. The market leader is now talking about expansion into Tier 3 cities. What is your 
experience there? So do you think that there is some more juice to kind of get in? One thing we 
are kind of noticing right, that whoever kind of acquires the customer first seems to kind of get 
the benefit of some sort of a loyalty rather than trying to acquire second and then you are 

 
 
 
 
Page 8 of 15 
 
basically also searching for the highest quality users. Does it not make sense for us to explore 
that at this point of time? 
Nandita Sinha: 
I think we have growth, which is near term largely, in the large cities. So that is where we are 
focused. Like I said, we are building the business and the focus towards execution on building 
on our habituated users. We do see a large part of our growth in the large cities. 
 
Therefore, we will continue to focus there. And like I said, we are not looking at geographical 
expansion beyond where we are today, and we will continue to focus on the all the cities that we 
are present in, and we will do that via the habituation that we have built by taking the users 
through this journey. That's where we will focus on. 
 
Our playbook for focusing on this journey remains the differentiated assortment that we are 
building. 1 in 8 orders today is of Noice, and that gives us a much higher retention. Similarly, as 
we build our pod productivity, that will give us a much higher advantage in terms of how we are 
growing. So these will continue to be our focus areas in the large cities that we are. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Understood. In terms of this quarter, there was obviously a timing difference in the festive season 
vis-a-vis last year. So would it be correct to think that the next quarter should see a much faster 
kind of growth or would you not rather kind of commit a higher number at this point of time? 
Nandita Sinha: 
Right now, we won't comment as we are in the beginning of the quarter.  
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Understood. And just one last question on food delivery. You are obviously sticking to the 
guidance of 18-20% YoY growth for the full year in the core business. Now one thing that I 
would like to understand is one way of doing that would be just to keep the margin flat and 
reinvest into growth. Is there a margin target that you have in mind where you start doing that 
or r would you just rather allow it to kind of continue the way it has been expanded ? 
Rahul Bothra: 
As you have seen, we've added close to INR50 crores on an absolute Adjusted EBITDA for the 
quarter and in a market where competition from all forms is only going higher. 5% of GOV 
trajectory is an outcome which is what we have stated. And you should continue to see operating 
leverage in our business, which we continue to accrue. 
 
At the same time, you may have seen our monetization, it is at the highest ever with take rate 
exceeding 26%. So there are sufficient levers which are available to us to be able to continue 
this journey to 5% and that's something that we are committed to. 
 
Beyond that, I think we start making choices around reinvesting back for growth because I don't 
think the margin journey necessarily stops at 5%. There is continued densification that happens 
, cost synergies that come through as well as operating leverage that you should expect in the 
results. 
Abhisek Banerjee: 
Got it. And just one last thing. Could you give any demographic profiles of the Swiggy core 
users versus the Toing users, if there is any differential that can be noted? 

 
 
 
 
Page 9 of 15 
 
Rohit Kapoor: 
We don't collect that much demographic data. But from our consumer dipsticks and 
understanding, the Swiggy platform caters to a pretty much a wide demographic starting right 
from the adolescents for whom the order is made by maybe the parent or elder sibling to right 
up to senior citizens.  
Our sense is that for Toing, the audience is far younger. And probably 70-80% of the users are 
sub 30 years of age and many of whom are coming into either they are in the final years of 
college or coming into employment and first-time jobbers and who will form the consuming 
class 3-5 years out, right, in a significant way. I think that's the difference that we see. 
Moderator: 
Your next question comes from the line of Jignanshu Gor with Bernstein. 
Jignanshu Gor: 
I had two questions. One for Nandita on quick commerce. So, one of the things that I see which 
is markedly different between our performance and the performance of the other listed peer is 
the monetization rate. I wanted to understand your plan to improve this and where do you think 
is the key issue because this rate has not really moved in the last 3 quarters. 
 
And I would sort of also expect that this is a project or effort which can run in parallel to the 
scale up, right, while there is some dependency. So I just want to understand how you are 
thinking about improving monetization for our quick commerce orders. 
Nandita Sinha: 
Thanks for the question. This is something that we are actually quite focused on in terms of 
building on two counts. I think as we look at our strategy in terms of engaging with brands on 
differentiated assortment, it allows us the opportunity to co-create with brands and that increases 
our engagement with them. 
 
On the other hand, I would say that also our ability to have a better set of users and more 
productivity on our pods, puts us in the flywheel with growth, especially for users and 
geographies, which we can then actually build together with brands. 
 
So, if you look at the loop that we are creating with differentiated assortment as well as by 
creating a high habit user, it allows us to engage better with our brands and therefore, take up 
our monetization rates. We've made some movement in this quarter. And we will continue to 
work on this stream because this allows us to give a great assortment to our customers as we 
work together with brands. So, this is something we focus on. 
Jignanshu Gor: 
So, there are two parts to this monetization, right, or three parts rather. There is commissions, 
there is ads simplistically and then there is income from consumers or charges. Where do you 
think we have the maximum leeway in these three and maybe the lower-hanging fruit as well?  
Nandita Sinha: 
I spoke about how we are co-creating with our brand partners. And that allows us to build the 
base for ensuring that monetization leads this growth. Over a period of time, we will ensure we 
will continue to evolve the consumer fees. The two parts that I would really focus on is 
monetization. The second thing is how are we evolving the consumer fee structure as we are 
evolving the habituated user. Monetization will need it and our co-creation with brands will help 
us actually build a more stickier user base, which we can then build habit over a period, which 

 
 
 
 
Page 10 of 15 
 
allows mix impact to be favourable for us as users become sticky. So this is where we will build 
this journey on. 
Jignanshu Gor: 
I think my second and last question is on Toing. And I think either Harsha or Rohit, I want to 
understand what's your framework for deciding, as you said, maybe in the next few quarters, 
whether Toing is an experiment, whether it's supposed to be scaled.  Like what are the metrics 
you're looking for? And what are you willing to compromise on? So is it the growth and the size 
of the market that you see which makes you attractive? 
 
Is it consumer behaviour? Is it the unit economics and is there a threshold for that? Are you 
willing to accept dilution to the margin profile of the food delivery business when you add the 
two businesses together? How are you thinking about your framework for decision-making on 
Toing? I think that will be helpful to understand. 
Sriharsha Majety: 
Harsha here. I think it is not just one thing, it is a set of the few. We've talked about how some 
of the early cities are showing what they are in unit economics for repeat users. We would like 
to see how that sustains. As we go and expand the user footprint, how does customer acquisition 
cost evolve. There are also continuous learnings that we are making in terms of propositions that 
can bring delivery costs even lower. And those are things that is some more advertisement push 
that will really help us get a more robust sense of the steady-state economics. 
Jignanshu Gor: 
Okay. So is it fair to say that we have a sort of an answer of what this can lead to, but we just 
need a few quarters to get there? Or is it that we are still discovering? So how early are we in 
that journey? I think that's the only second thing which would be helpful. 
Sriharsha Majety: 
As we mentioned, I think at this stage, with the state of the business that is four quarters old, 
we're quite happy with the progress that it's made. As Rahul mentioned, majority of the spend is 
in marketing user activities, which means it is discretionary.  
And we are in a competitive market. We want to really understand more about the stuff that we 
are already building conviction on, I'd say because we will know if it can be profitable over the 
next few quarters, that we'll get a better sense of the levers that we originally envisaged for the 
steady-state economics getting more information on that. Things will be competitive, but we'll 
still be able to get a good sense of how the model can work.  
Rohit Kapoor: 
Adding on to what Harsha said, there is clear evidence in the food delivery we have used in the 
past that scale turns into margins and EBITDA over a period of time, and we have demonstrated 
that successfully. We see no reason why that same thing will not play out in Toing. Of course, 
there's an investment needed to create a business of this size and to push the growth rates from, 
let's say, 18-20%, which was envisaged earlier to 25-30% what we have seen. 
 
As we have said even in the shareholders’ letter, we expect the investments will be range bound. 
And we'll operate with all three guardrails in terms of building the business. One is, is it opening 
up new TAM, which it is at this point in time. Second, is the consumer showing the right amount 
of retention frequency, which is there at this point in time. 

 
 
 
 
Page 11 of 15 
 
 
And third is shaping the economics towards what becomes a hopefully very profitable business 
over a period of time. There will be a bit of a curve for sure. But I think there's nothing that we 
see at this point in time, which discourages us from just pushing ahead of this.
